allup/rewards: A grader scores four answers a model sampled for one question, from zero to one: zero point nine, zero point six, zero point five and zero point two.
allup/allup: Every reward is positive, so the policy gradient pushes every one of these answers up, even the worst. Only the size of the push differs.
allup/noise: On average the good answers still win, but each estimate is noisy: whatever happens to be sampled gets pushed up.
baseline/b: So subtract a baseline, b: the reward you expected. Here, the average of the four, zero point five five.
baseline/A: What is left is the advantage, A, equal to R minus b: zero point three five, zero point zero five, minus zero point zero five and minus zero point three five.
baseline/signs: Use A in place of R. Now the answers that beat expectations are pushed up, and the rest are pushed down.
baseline/third: Look at the third answer. Its reward, zero point five, is positive, but below what was expected, so now it gets pushed down.
same/sum: Why is this allowed? Average the gradient of log pi over the model's answers. pi times the gradient of its log is just the gradient of pi.
same/one: And the probabilities always add up to one, so their gradients add up to zero: they cannot all rise at once.
same/zero: So the baseline's share of the estimate, b times the gradient of log pi, averages to zero. The expected direction stays the same; only the noise drops.
same/best: The best baseline is the reward you expect for that very question: a running average of past rewards works, or a second model trained to predict it.
